title: 105 Lawmakers Demand FBI Hate-Crime Probe Into Foiled Aurora Hindu Temple Shooting
excerpt: Led by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was inside the Aurora Balaji temple with his family during the October 11 attempt, Congress members gave FBI Director Kash Patel until October 29 to answer on bias, online threats and temple protection.
body:
• 105 members of Congress, led by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, have written to FBI Director Kash Patel demanding the October 11 Aurora temple attack attempt be investigated as a potential federal hate crime.
  • Krishnamoorthi and his family were worshipping at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, when 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis allegedly tried to shoot a man outside; his rifle jammed.
  • The lawmakers set an October 29, 2026 deadline for the FBI's written answers on bias, online threats and protection for houses of worship.
  • Temple congregations can expect the letter to put federal threat-sharing and protective outreach for South Asian houses of worship on the record within days.

The new development in the Aurora temple case is a number: 105. That is how many members of Congress signed a letter to FBI Director Kash Patel urging the Bureau to investigate the attempted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, as a potential federal hate crime, according to a statement from Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi's office. The letter, reported by ANI via Devdiscourse, was led by Krishnamoorthi and includes the entire Illinois House Democratic delegation, every Indian American member of Congress, and Senators Dick Durbin, Tammy Duckworth, Andy Kim and Chris Van Hollen.

Krishnamoorthi's presence gives the letter its weight. He and his family were worshipping at the temple when the attempted attack occurred on October 11, during the Navaratri season.

What prosecutors allege happened on October 11

According to prosecutors, 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis, a self-identified neo-Nazi, tried to shoot a man outside the temple, but his rifle jammed. He fled and later communicated plans to return before a coworker alerted police, who arrested him that day. Prosecutors allege that he authored an eight-page white supremacist manifesto describing violence against people of Indian descent at a Hindu house of worship. Investigators recovered a rifle, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, body armor, and white supremacist imagery. He faces state charges including making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a firearm.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=tDvaZ_w9RhA

"The alleged combination of targeted racial hatred, a religious setting, and preparations for mass violence demands a comprehensive federal response."

— Letter from 105 members of Congress to FBI Director Kash Patel

Five questions, and a deadline

The letter does more than ask for a hate-crime investigation. It puts five written questions to the FBI and requests answers, to the extent consistent with an ongoing investigation, by October 29, 2026. The lawmakers ask whether the Bureau is examining both racial or ethnic bias and religious bias, and whether it is coordinating with the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division and the US Attorney's Office. They ask whether investigators are examining online platforms the defendant may have used to communicate threats, select targets or obtain assistance, and whether anyone encouraged or materially assisted the alleged plot.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2112771492316385486

They also ask what mechanisms exist for sharing actionable threat information with state and local law enforcement and with potentially targeted houses of worship, what outreach and protective resources are being offered to affected communities, and whether the FBI has adequate personnel, language expertise and analytical capacity to assess threats involving anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian bias.

The climate the letter cites

The lawmakers ground their demand in data. A September 2026 report identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026, with monthly volume rising approximately 240 percent from January 2024 to June 2026. A Carnegie Endowment survey found that 48 percent of Indian American respondents encountered racist posts targeting their community very or somewhat often since the start of 2025, while one in four reported being called a slur.

The letter also criticizes Trump administration messaging that the signers warn risks legitimizing racial and religious stereotypes, citing a Department of Homeland Security post depicting a Sikh man with the message, "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr. Singh," and a Department of Education post declaring "Make College Football Great Again" after a Texas Republican complained about South Asians attending a University of Texas football game. Federal agencies, the lawmakers wrote, should make clear that debates over immigration or public safety never justify collective suspicion of Indian, Sikh, Hindu or other South Asian communities.

What this means for congregations

For Hindu, Sikh and Jain congregations across the US, the practical stake is the answer to the letter's fourth question: how threat information reaches temples before an attack, not after one. A federal hate-crime designation would also change the resources and sentencing exposure attached to the Aurora case itself. The lawmakers close with the sentence that frames the whole intervention: no congregation should have to wonder whether gathering for worship will make its members targets of mass violence. The FBI's response is due by October 29.
